newsitem.title: MALI: FEATURE-Echoes of Live Aid as Uncle Sam helps Liberia.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Echoes of Live Aid as Uncle Sam helps Liberia.

text.p: In a broiling hangar in a dusty corner of Africa a tiny crop survey plane emblazoned with the words "Love From Live Aid" recalls the rock world's 1980s charity appeal to save millions from famine or war.

Outside in the shimmering heat, American special forces swarm around cavernous C130 transport planes airlifting over 600 Malian peacekeepers and equipment to Liberia -- which is preparing for elections to end seven years of civil war.
Each operation in its own way is an attempt to bandage Africa's wounds -- albeit a decade apart.

"We're moving everything from water tanks to goats," said Major Vic Warzinski, Public Affairs liaison for "Operation Assured Lift" -- a U.S.-sponsored airlift of over 1,000 West African troops which started on February 15 and is expected to end this week.
Liberia has strong emotional ties with the United States. Freed American slaves founded the republic in 1847.
The West African peacekeepers heading for Liberia's capital Monrovia include up to 600 Ghanaians and 600 Malians, up to 100 Ivorian medics -- and a Ghanaian regimental goat.
"The Ghanaian troops had to have their mascot. It was very important to them," Warzinski added.
FIRST WORLD SOLUTIONS
The peacekeepers' task is to hold a line between Liberia's factions after disarmament which ended early in February and during the countdown to national elections on May 30.
Malian troops with Soviet-made Kalashnikovs line up between mothballed MiG fighter planes -- another echo from the past.
Across the tarmac, technicians from the world's one remaining superpower battle in Third World conditions to repair an engine that threatens to delay the operation.
They have help. A dishevelled Malian corporal surrounded by grim faced U.S. special forces sweats over an ancient Chinese lathe to retool a tiny oil pump part.
"We also mend carts," he smiled, pointing to a pile of dusty hand-drawn barrows as he retooled a tiny oil pump part.
In the end, the U.S. airforce flew in a new engine.
"The problem is that we are 2,000 miles (3,200 km) away from our maintenance base," explains Air Expeditionary Group Commander Colonel Michael Smith.
The airlift was originally scheduled to last two weeks but now the U.S. airforce is on African time. "We expected the operation to last two weeks but you can never tell," Smith adds.
As the sun moves across the sky, Green Beret Special Forces watch and wait. They are anxious to be on their way.
"We have a security problem here," says one Green Beret Captain. Delays mean taking a convoy of Malians across Monrovia at night rather than during daylight.
"Assured Lift" is now scheduled to end on March 5.
UNINVITED GUEST
An Algerian Hercules provides a touch of light relief, raising eyebrows as it taxies into the temporary American compound. It turns and leaves.
"Maybe they've come to help the Americans," says one Malian officer -- an idea quickly scotched by a U.S. political hand.
"Oops, I think I am in the wrong place," he later quoted a passenger as saying in perfect English.
Malian forces finally begin loading Egyptian-built Armoured Personnel Carriers, ZU-23 anti-aircraft guns, water tankers, medical trucks -- and pallets of televisions.
At one point three out of five C-130s were delayed by technical hitches. One plane set off half a day late, the plane with the engine problem was due out even later.
WARM WELCOME?
Presidential hopeful Charles Taylor, who launched the war in late 1989, was on hand when the first Hercules flight arrived at Liberia's Robertsfield airport a couple of days earlier.
"It was quite a welcoming party but totally unexpected," says Warzinski. "There were about 150 dancers and musicians so I guess he just wanted to make a statement."
Taylor, in fact, was leaving on a trip to Taiwan.
The peacekeepers will boost the 10,000-strong West African peacekeeping force ECOMOG, which is supervising implementation of a peace deal brokered by Liberia's leaders last August.
"After eight years of war we hope the Liberian warlords will be weary," muses Souleyman Cisse, second in command of the Malian battalion.
Charles Taylor, once a strident critic of the role of the Nigerian-led peacekeeping force and likely election front-runner, has, meanwhile, had a change of heart.
Having heard that the peacekeepers only plan to stay for six months after the installation of a new government, he has suggested they stay longer -- to ensure a peaceful transition.
U.S. involvement, for the time being, is limited to the airlift.
